title: Narrioch (Gravesend Neck)
summary: Narrioch is a Kings County placename associated with Gravesend Neck, interpreted as a point or corner of land. The name is tied to the same 1654 release that names Mannahanning.
map_geometry_source: approximate modern Gravesend Neck marker, offset slightly from nearby Gravesend Neck placename for map visibility; not exact historical coordinate
history_content:
Narrioch belongs to the Gravesend Neck landscape in present-day Brooklyn. It is closely related to Mannahanning / Coney Island, with time-specific documentary context shown through Historic Moments.

A point of land

Guttaquoh’s release of 1654 names Narrioch with Mannahanning. Tooker read Narrioch as “a point of land,” describing the neck that ends in a point.

William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911), printed p. 153.

During Kieft’s War, war parties attacked the young English settlement at Gravesend founded by Lady Deborah Moody; about forty settlers from nearby farms gathered at her house to hold them off.

John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700 (Empire State Books, 1997), printed p. 182.
translation_content:
Narrioch is interpreted as a point of land or corner land, connecting the form with language for a point or corner and a land/place ending. Related spellings include Narriock and Narrioch.

Why Place Names Matter

“Thus, through geographical names, we can learn about geography, society, construction, history and culture of a region or country.”

— Le Minh Tam, Preserving and promoting the historical-cultural value of geographical names (2015), UNGEGN Information Bulletin No. 48, PDF page 17
whereintheworld_content: The map shows an approximate location for Gravesend Neck in Brooklyn, moved slightly from another Gravesend Neck placename marker so each can be seen and is not an exact boundary for the older neck landscape.
